title: Love Canal: Even Dirtier Than It Sounds
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) cover the Love Canal toxic waste disaster in Niagara Falls, New York. They trace the origin from William T. Love's abandoned model-city canal in the 1890s, through Hooker Chemical's burial of toxic waste and the 1953-era sale of the site to the city for one dollar and the school built on it, to the 1970s crisis of leaking chemicals, black sludge, birth defects and miscarriages. They cover Lois Gibbs and the Love Canal Homeowners Association, Dr. Beverly Paigen's wet/dry home survey, state and federal responses including the 1978 health emergency, Jimmy Carter's emergency relocation funding, the 1980 CERCLA Superfund law, Hooker's settlement, and the later state of the neighborhood (Black Creek). The episode closes with a Flint documentary plug and a listener mail about patent medicines.
topics: wet homes and dry homes study

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on Love Canal as an American toxic waste incident that revealed ground pollution.

segments.title: William T. Love and the model city canal
segments.summary: William T. Love proposes a model city and a diverted Niagara River canal for hydroelectric power in the 1890s. The Panic of 1893 and Tesla's long-distance transmission end the project, and Love leaves for Ontario.

segments.title: Hooker Chemical buys the canal
segments.summary: In the 1930s Hooker Electrochemical Company buys the unfinished canal, about sixteen acres, and fills it with chemical waste including dioxins and PCBs, with the Army also dumping there.

segments.title: Sale to the city for one dollar and the school
segments.summary: Hooker caps the pit and sells the land to the City of Niagara Falls for one dollar. The Board of Education builds an elementary school on it despite warnings in the deed and from Hooker, and the school board goes ahead anyway.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Housing development and early health problems
segments.summary: The school opens in 1955 and about 800 houses and 240 apartments are built around it. Children suffer chemical burns in 1958, the Vorhees family finds black sludge in their basement, kids burn from white phosphorus rocks, and babies are born with birth defects. Wet and rising groundwater from harsh winters brings waste up into yards, and a pool and a ball field are affected.

segments.title: 1977 blizzard, Niagara Gazette and city cover-up
segments.summary: The 1976 Niagara Gazette article links the illnesses to Love Canal. After the 1977 blizzard, the city hires Calspan, whose investigators leave after data shows severe toxicity, but the city does not disclose the report.

segments.title: Tourism concerns and Phil Donahue
segments.summary: The city, fearing harm to tourism and angry at Hooker, tries to keep the problem quiet. Phil Donahue compares the mayor to the mayor from Jaws. Hosts briefly discuss Phil Hartman.

segments.title: Health commissioner dismisses residents; Lois Gibbs begins organizing
segments.summary: Health commissioner Dr. Francis Clifford calls residents hypochondriacs. Lois Gibbs, a mother with a high school education, tries to pull her son from the school, is refused, and founds the Love Canal Homeowners Association.

segments.title: Symptoms and New York State investigation
segments.summary: Residents report birth defects, cancers, liver and kidney problems. The New York State Health Department investigates in 1978 and finds high miscarriage rates among other problems.
topics: New York State Health Department investigation

segments.title: Health emergency declared
segments.summary: In August 1978 state Health Commissioner Robert Whalen declares a health emergency and advises pregnant women and families with children under two to leave. Residents, many tied to mortgages, cannot easily leave, and property values collapse.

segments.title: Federal emergency and buyouts
segments.summary: President Jimmy Carter declares a federal emergency and provides ten million dollars. New York Governor Carey agrees to buy 239 homes in the first rings and close the school. Hosts note this was the first federal emergency funding for a non-natural disaster.

segments.title: Residents left out of buyouts
segments.summary: Residents outside the first two rings are told they are fine and denied relief, restarting the fight. Lois Gibbs lives in the second zone and keeps organizing.

segments.title: Community division and wet homes study
segments.summary: Remaining residents are viewed as troublemakers by the rest of the city. The LHCA and Dr. Beverly Paigen conduct a door-to-door health survey finding higher birth defects, asthma and suicide attempts in wet homes near creeks and swales, dismissed by authorities as housewife data.

segments.title: Paigen's analysis of buried creek beds
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the national average birth defect rate and explain that Paigen showed buried creek beds moved contaminated water to homes beyond the dump, risking her career.

segments.title: EPA involvement, hostage incident and Superfund law
segments.summary: The EPA tests the area and confirms the problems. Protesters take EPA officials hostage for about five hours. In October 1980 Carter approves more funding and relocation of remaining families. Congress passes CERCLA, the Superfund law, creating a trust fund and a national priorities list; Love Canal lands on the list in 1983.

segments.title: Cleanup, Hooker lawsuit and settlement
segments.summary: Remediation takes decades and costs about 350 million dollars, with a clay cap, groundwater treatment and monitoring wells. The EPA sues Hooker in 1979; Hooker settles in the 1990s for about 227 million dollars without admitting fault.

segments.title: Black Creek today and new residents
segments.summary: The neighborhood is rebuilt as Black Creek and new residents move in, often unaware of the history. The waste was covered rather than removed.

segments.title: Recent lawsuits and health data
segments.summary: Twenty lawsuits with about 700 plaintiffs were filed in recent years, and a state judge dismissed major cases in 2023. Studies show cancer rates lower but birth defects about twice as high as nearby communities.

segments.title: Lois Gibbs' legacy
segments.summary: Lois Gibbs founds the Center for Health, Environment and Justice to help small towns handle toxic sites. Hosts joke about her.
topics: Center for Health, Environment and Justice

segments.title: Reading suggestions
segments.summary: Hosts suggest listeners look online for more on Love Canal.

segments.title: Flint documentary plug
segments.summary: Iheart Intro promotes a friend's documentary about the Flint, Michigan water poisoning, and hosts agree Flint deserves its own episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: patent medicines
segments.summary: A listener corrects the snake oil episode, explaining patents require disclosing the invention and noting most patent medicines did not actually hold patents.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the listener mail address and the show credit.
